u u_n+(\operatorname{div}
u)u_n=0$ hold classically, where $u_n=u\cdot
u$ and the normal is extended constant along collar normal lines. This includes zero eigenvalues and disconnected domains; it asserts neither equality with every maximal tangential-trace realization nor smoothness of arbitrary finite-energy modal sums.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the weak-solvability and regularity lemmas below ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain in the local graph sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}^3)$ be uniformly positive, that is $\alpha|\xi|^2\le\xi\cdot\varepsilon(x)\xi\le eta|\xi|^2$ for all $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$ and $x\in\Omega$ and some $0<\alpha\le eta<\infty$, and let $ho$ be smooth on $\overline\Omega$. The Euclidean inner product is that of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; at a boundary point with outward unit normal $
u$ the outward conormal vector is $\varepsilon
u$ and the outward conormal derivative is $
u\cdot\varepsilon
abla u$. Here $H^1(\Omega)$ and $H_0^1(\Omega)$ are the Sobolev spaces of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and the trace $T$ is that of the trace operator on the bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega$. Then:

(a) **Dirichlet.** For every $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ there is exactly one weak solution $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ with trace $Tu=g$ of $\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot\varepsilon
abla u\,dx=\int_\Omegaho v\,dx$ for all $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$; it depends continuously on the data, $\|u\|_{H^1}\le C(\|ho\|_{L^2}+\|g\|_{H^{1/2}})$, has a $C^\infty$ representative on $\overline\Omega$, and satisfies the classical equations $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon
abla u)=ho$ in $\Omega$ and $u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$.

(b) **Neumann.** Let $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ be a smooth outward conormal datum satisfying $\int_{\Omega_j}ho\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega_j}g\,dS=0$ on every connected component $\Omega_j$ of $\Omega$. Then there is a weak solution of $\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot\varepsilon
abla u=\int_\Omegaho v+\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,Tv$ for all $v\in H^1(\Omega)$; it is unique up to a separately chosen additive constant on each component, and imposing $\int_{\Omega_j}u=0$ on every component gives a unique normalised solution which is $C^\infty$ on each closed component and satisfies the classical equations $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon
abla u)=ho$ in $\Omega$ and $
u\cdot\varepsilon
abla u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$. In particular on a connected domain the compatibility is $\int_{\partial\Omega}g=-\int_\Omegaho$, with a single additive constant.

(c) **Transmission.** Let there be finitely many pairwise disjoint closed smooth interfaces strictly inside $\Omega$, let $\varepsilon$ be piecewise smooth on the closures of the resulting pieces and uniformly positive in the above sense, let $ho$ be piecewise smooth on the closed pieces and let $\sigma$ be a smooth sheet charge on the union of the interfaces; the weak right-hand side is $\int_\Omegaho v+\sum_\Gamma\int_\Gamma\sigma\,Tv$, together with $\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,Tv$ in the Neumann case. Prescribe either the smooth outer Dirichlet datum of (a), or the smooth outer Neumann datum of (b) with the componentwise compatibility condition $\int_{\Omega_j}ho+\sum_{\Gamma\subset\Omega_j}\int_\Gamma\sigma+\int_{\partial\Omega_j}g=0$ for every component $\Omega_j$. With outer Dirichlet data the globally $H^1$ solution is unique; with outer Neumann data it exists exactly when that compatibility holds and is then unique modulo componentwise additive constants, the zero componentwise means making it unique; the equal one-sided traces and $C^\infty$ regularity on each closed side hold in either case, and the flux jump is $n\cdot[\varepsilon
abla u]=-\sigma$ in the sign convention of [[lem-em-weak-neumann-and-transmission-existence]], where $n$ is a chosen unit normal on the interface and $[\varepsilon
abla u]=\varepsilon^+
abla u^+-\varepsilon^-
abla u^-$ is the difference from the $n$-positive side to the other.

Edge and junction points, reentrant corners, coefficient loss of regularity and general piecewise classical regularity beyond finitely many disjoint smooth interfaces are excluded. The existence content of all three parts is that of the two weak solvability lemmas; this theorem states the combined existence-and-regularity conclusions on the declared domains and adds no existence assertion beyond them.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L_j>0$ and let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ be constants. Define the reflection boundary class by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2,x_3$-walls, and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$; extend $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$, cyclically for $B_2,B_3$. Work on the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$ in the real $L^2$ fields with these parities and distributional $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$. For smooth fields the parity class gives $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on $\partial Q$. Then: (i) the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in this class, and the class is complete for the $L^2$ pairing ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]); (ii) for every initial datum in the class there is a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the same class ([[def-distributional-derivative]]); (iii) the energy $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ is constant along the solution. This is an explicit weak PEC model; it supplies neither trace regularity for arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ fields nor completeness in lossy, open or non-rectangular guides.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ in the graph sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]; connectedness is unnecessary. Write $H^m(\Omega)=W^{m,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with the multi-index integral norm ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) and $H_0^1(\Omega)$ for the $H^1$ closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). For every real $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ there is a unique $u\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap H^2(\Omega)$ satisfying

$$\int_\Omega(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+uv)=\int_\Omega fv\qquad(v\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

It satisfies $(1-\Delta)u=f$ distributionally and almost everywhere as an $L^2$ identity, and

$$\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad\|u\|_{H^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$

Moreover $D=\{\varphi\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega):\varphi|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$ is dense in $H^2(\Omega)\cap H_0^1(\Omega)$ in the $H^2$ norm: every such $w$ has $\varphi_j\in D$ with $\varphi_j\to w$ in $H^2$. Here smoothness on the closure means restriction of a smooth function on a neighbourhood of the closure, equivalently the smooth chart representatives used below. In particular $\nabla\varphi_j\to\nabla w$ in the graph norm of $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$, with zero curl and $\operatorname{div}\nabla w=\Delta w$; every $\nabla\varphi_j$ is smooth and PEC since its tangential derivatives vanish at the boundary. For precision, let $X_\Omega$ be the graph-norm closure of smooth vector fields on a neighbourhood of the closure with $\nu\times v=0$ on the boundary, where $\nu$ is the outward Euclidean unit normal. The ambient graph space consists of real $L^2$ vector fields whose distributional $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_i\partial_iv_i$ and $\operatorname{curl}v=(\partial_2v_3-\partial_3v_2,\partial_3v_1-\partial_1v_3,\partial_1v_2-\partial_2v_1)$ lie in $L^2$; its norm squared is $\|v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2$. Thus $\nabla w$ belongs to this explicitly defined $X_\Omega$, the same completion used by the later cavity item. No equality with every maximal trace realisation is asserted.

No smoothness of $f$, no classical boundary value for general $u$, and no general nonsmooth-domain, Neumann, interface, or variable-coefficient claim is included. Zero boundary condition means membership in $H_0^1$; the published trace theorem identifies its trace as zero.

derivations.claim: **The definitions agree and the cavity conclusions apply.** The class $X$, the subspace $V$ and the space $H$ of the Statement are exactly those of [L1] for the same domain $\Omega$: the same graph-norm closure of the same smooth fields on the closure with $\nu\times u=0$, the same divergence-free subspace and the same closed $L^2$ span, and the Axiom of Choice assumed in the Statement is the choice assumption of [L1], whose meaning is fixed by [L5]. Hence all conclusions of [L1] hold in the present setting: the curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis $\{u_j\}$ with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity and $\lambda_j\to\infty$ whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, the zero eigenspace is finite dimensional and retained, each eigenfield satisfies the full $X$ variational identity and the distributional eigen-equation with the PEC trace, and the modal wave expansion with the chosen positive speed $v_{\mathrm{wave}}$ has the stated initial coefficients, the stated continuities on compact intervals and affine zero modes.

**Rectangular class.** [L4] states exactly the assertions of part (b) for the reflection boundary class with constants $\varepsilon,\mu>0$: density of the finite separated Fourier modes at every time, unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solutions of the two equations in the class for every initial datum, and constancy of $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$. Its Countable Choice hypothesis is available in the present setting: the Statement assumes the Axiom of Choice, and the implication to Countable Choice is the choice supplier [L5].

**Smooth eigenfields.** Fix $j$. By step 1.1, $u_j\in X$, $\operatorname{div}u_j=0$ weakly and the full $X$ variational identity holds for $u_j$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$; hence the hypotheses of [L2] are satisfied and $u_j\in H^m(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ for every integer $m\ge1$ with a $C^\infty$ representative on $\overline\Omega$, for which the classical relations $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$, $\operatorname{div}u_j=0$, $
u	imes u_j=0$ and $\partial_
u u_{j,n}+(\operatorname{div}
u)u_{j,n}=0$ hold, with $u_{j,n}=u_j\cdot
u$ and $
u$ extended constant along collar normal lines; the Euclidean pairing and the reading of the differentiated identities are those of [L6]. In particular the zero eigenvalues $\lambda_j=0$ are included and no eigenfield is discarded.

**Exact scalar auxiliary boundary problem.** The actual divergence-preservation argument in [L1] sets $q=\operatorname{div}K_0f\in L^2$ and uses $(1-\Delta)\varphi=q$ with $\varphi\in H_0^1\cap H^2$. Its existence and the admissible smooth zero-boundary approximation of $\nabla\varphi$ are exactly [L7], so the full graph-class identity can be passed to this rough-data test without assuming that $q$ is smooth. If $q$ is smooth, the boundary quotient argument recorded in [L7] and the smooth-domain bootstrap behind [L3] apply with the additional zeroth-order term $+\varphi$: tangential differentiation creates only lower-order derivatives of $\varphi$, which are already controlled at each induction stage, and normal recovery uses the positive coefficient of $\partial_{nn}\varphi$ as before. Starting from the $H^2$ solution, induction gives every $H^m$, hence the smooth representative on the closure; the unchanged lower-order term requires no new boundary data. Independently, [L3] supplies the classical upgrade for smooth unshifted Poisson Dirichlet or compatible Neumann problems with $\varepsilon=I$. The vector eigenfield upgrade is still supplied by [L2], and no smoothness of the actual rough auxiliary datum is used in spectral closure.

**Assembly, exclusions and choice accounting.** Part (a) is steps 1.1, 2.1 and 2.2: step 1.1 transfers the spectral completeness, multiplicity, growth, zero-mode retention, full-$X$ identity, distributional eigen-equation and modal wave expansion from [L1]; step 2.1 upgrades every eigenfield to a $C^\infty$ field on the closure satisfying the classical PEC relations, including the zero eigenvalues; and step 2.2 records the exact rough-data $H^2$ resolvent and graph-density prerequisite [L7], its smooth-data bootstrap, and the separate smooth unshifted scalar upgrade [L3]. Part (b) is step 1.2, which is [L4] verbatim in the present notation. Nothing outside the declared classes is asserted: no lossy, open-ended or non-smooth spectral completeness, no identification with every maximal tangential-trace realisation, and no physical reading of the abstract speed $v_{\mathrm{wave}}$; the constant-Ohmic and open-longitudinal branches are homed on the guide page as separate physical items and are not used here. The Axiom of Choice is used only through [L1]–[L3] and, through its Countable Choice consequence [L5], through [L4]; no other choice principle and no choice of data beyond the explicit open set $\{v_{\mathrm{wave}}>0\}$ occurs. This proves all assertions.

boundaries.evidence: Initial data q_0=0, q_1=0 give the zero displacement and velocity through the modal coefficients of step 1.1; no other empty object is charged.

The zero eigenvalue sector is retained: step 1.1 keeps the finite-dimensional lambda=0 eigenspace with affine modes a_j(t)=a_j(0)+t a_j'(0), and step 2.1 applies the eigenfield boundary regularity to lambda=0 fields.

If H is finite dimensional the eigenbasis of step 1.1 is finite; the growth assertion lambda_j to infinity is made only when H is infinite dimensional, so the one-mode case is covered without a false limit claim.

Degenerate sectors are covered explicitly: the rectangular class of step 1.2 includes the zero wavevector and the reflection-parity data of [L4], and the smooth class of step 1.1 retains zero eigenvalues.

The obstacle boundary and the artificial sphere are interior to the arguments: step 2.1 gives the classical boundary relations on the closed domain, and no decay or asymptotic behaviour at infinity is used.
The Axiom of Choice is assumed in the statement; steps 1.1 and 2.1 consume it through [L1]-[L3], and step 1.2 obtains the Countable Choice of [L4] through the implication [L5].

boundaries.reason: The theorem asserts spectral completeness, regularity and unique weak solvability inside the declared classes; no biconditional criterion with a forward direction is asserted.
No converse is asserted: the theorem does not characterise which classes admit complete spectral decompositions, and it makes no claim in the excluded lossy, open or non-smooth classes.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

For $r\ge0$, put $\overline B_3(0,r):=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, extending the positive-radius notation of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] to $r=0$. This closed three-dimensional ball has volume $4\pi r^3/3$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ vanish outside $\overline B_a(0)$. Use the complete orthonormal basis $\{Y_{lm}\}$ of real spherical harmonics on $S^2$ with unnormalised surface measure $d\sigma$ of total mass $4\pi$ and the addition theorem of [[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]], and the Legendre generating kernel and its compact remainder bound from [[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]. Write $x=rn$, $r=|x|$, $n\in S^2$. Then:

(a) **Exterior multipole expansion.** For every $x$ with $|x|>a$, $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy=\sum_{l=0}^\infty\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\frac{Y_{lm}(n)}{r^{l+1}}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^lY_{lm}(y/|y|)\rho(y)\,dy,$$ the series converging absolutely and uniformly on $\{|x|\ge r_0\}$ for every $r_0>a$, with tail after degree $N$ bounded by $\|\rho\|_1\,a^{N+1}/(r_0^{N+2}(1-a/r_0))$; for every fixed $r>a$, the degree-$l$ term is the $L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$ angular projection of $n\mapsto F_r(n):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|rn-y|^{-1}\rho(y)\,dy$ onto the degree-$l$ harmonics. This function is continuous and bounded by $\|\rho\|_1/(r-a)$, so it is in $L^2(S^2)$; no sphere trace or $L^2$ property of the volume density $\rho$ is asserted. The degree-zero and degree-one terms are the Coulomb and dipole terms with the explicit remainder bound of [[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]] ($Q=\int\rho$, $p=\int y\rho(y)\,dy$, $|R(x)|\le16a^2\|\rho\|_1/|x|^3$ for $|x|\ge2a$).

(b) **Termwise differentiation.** On every compact $K$ with $\inf_K|x|>a$ the series may be differentiated termwise to every order, the differentiated series converging uniformly on $K$; in particular the potential is $C^\infty$ on $\{|x|>a\}$.

(c) **Ball boundary branch.** For $f\in L^2(S^2)$ with coefficients $f_{lm}$ the series $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}r^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ converges in $L^2(S^2)$ as $r\uparrow1$ and, with all derivatives, uniformly on each closed ball of radius $<1$, is harmonic on the open unit ball, and is the unique harmonic function there with a finite $\sup_{r<1}\|u(r\cdot)\|_2$ and $L^2$ boundary limit $f$; for continuous $f$ it equals the Poisson integral $(1-r^2)/(4\pi|rn-n'|^3)$ of $f$ and extends continuously to the closed ball with boundary values $f$.

This is a statement about the Newtonian integral of a compactly supported $L^1$ density and about harmonic functions; no physical charge distribution or electrostatic interpretation is asserted. In every coefficient integral the factor $|y|^lY_{lm}(y/|y|)$ is defined at $y=0$ by its homogeneous polynomial extension: zero for $l\ge1$ and the constant degree-zero harmonic for $l=0$. This is a finite assignment, and changing its value at that null singleton changes no integral.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the weak-solvability and regularity lemmas below ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain in the local graph sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}^3)$ be uniformly positive, that is $\alpha|\xi|^2\le\xi\cdot\varepsilon(x)\xi\le eta|\xi|^2$ for all $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$ and $x\in\Omega$ and some $0<\alpha\le eta<\infty$, and let $ho$ be smooth on $\overline\Omega$. The Euclidean inner product is that of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; at a boundary point with outward unit normal $
u$ the outward conormal vector is $\varepsilon
u$ and the outward conormal derivative is $
u\cdot\varepsilon
abla u$. Here $H^1(\Omega)$ and $H_0^1(\Omega)$ are the Sobolev spaces of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and the trace $T$ is that of the trace operator on the bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega$. Then:

(a) **Dirichlet.** For every $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ there is exactly one weak solution $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ with trace $Tu=g$ of $\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot\varepsilon
abla u\,dx=\int_\Omegaho v\,dx$ for all $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$; it depends continuously on the data, $\|u\|_{H^1}\le C(\|ho\|_{L^2}+\|g\|_{H^{1/2}})$, has a $C^\infty$ representative on $\overline\Omega$, and satisfies the classical equations $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon
abla u)=ho$ in $\Omega$ and $u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$.

(b) **Neumann.** Let $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ be a smooth outward conormal datum satisfying $\int_{\Omega_j}ho\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega_j}g\,dS=0$ on every connected component $\Omega_j$ of $\Omega$. Then there is a weak solution of $\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot\varepsilon
abla u=\int_\Omegaho v+\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,Tv$ for all $v\in H^1(\Omega)$; it is unique up to a separately chosen additive constant on each component, and imposing $\int_{\Omega_j}u=0$ on every component gives a unique normalised solution which is $C^\infty$ on each closed component and satisfies the classical equations $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon
abla u)=ho$ in $\Omega$ and $
u\cdot\varepsilon
abla u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$. In particular on a connected domain the compatibility is $\int_{\partial\Omega}g=-\int_\Omegaho$, with a single additive constant.

(c) **Transmission.** Let there be finitely many pairwise disjoint closed smooth interfaces strictly inside $\Omega$, let $\varepsilon$ be piecewise smooth on the closures of the resulting pieces and uniformly positive in the above sense, let $ho$ be piecewise smooth on the closed pieces and let $\sigma$ be a smooth sheet charge on the union of the interfaces; the weak right-hand side is $\int_\Omegaho v+\sum_\Gamma\int_\Gamma\sigma\,Tv$, together with $\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,Tv$ in the Neumann case. Prescribe either the smooth outer Dirichlet datum of (a), or the smooth outer Neumann datum of (b) with the componentwise compatibility condition $\int_{\Omega_j}ho+\sum_{\Gamma\subset\Omega_j}\int_\Gamma\sigma+\int_{\partial\Omega_j}g=0$ for every component $\Omega_j$. With outer Dirichlet data the globally $H^1$ solution is unique; with outer Neumann data it exists exactly when that compatibility holds and is then unique modulo componentwise additive constants, the zero componentwise means making it unique; the equal one-sided traces and $C^\infty$ regularity on each closed side hold in either case, and the flux jump is $n\cdot[\varepsilon
abla u]=-\sigma$ in the sign convention of [[lem-em-weak-neumann-and-transmission-existence]], where $n$ is a chosen unit normal on the interface and $[\varepsilon
abla u]=\varepsilon^+
abla u^+-\varepsilon^-
abla u^-$ is the difference from the $n$-positive side to the other.

Edge and junction points, reentrant corners, coefficient loss of regularity and general piecewise classical regularity beyond finitely many disjoint smooth interfaces are excluded. The existence content of all three parts is that of the two weak solvability lemmas; this theorem states the combined existence-and-regularity conclusions on the declared domains and adds no existence assertion beyond them.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain in the local graph sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], with outward Euclidean unit normal field $\nu$ on $\partial\Omega$. Restate the class conventions of [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]]: $L^2:=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is the real Hilbert space of square integrable vector fields with the inner product $\langle u,v\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot v\,dx$ induced by the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and
$$H(\operatorname{curl})=\{u\in L^2:\operatorname{curl}u\in L^2\},\qquad H(\operatorname{div})=\{u\in L^2:\operatorname{div}u\in L^2\}$$
are the graph spaces with norms $\|u\|^2_{H(\operatorname{curl})}=\|u\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_2^2$ and $\|u\|^2_{H(\operatorname{div})}=\|u\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}u\|_2^2$, the curl and divergence being taken in the distributional sense; $X$ is the graph-norm closure in $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$ of the fields that are smooth on a neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$ and satisfy $\nu\times u=0$ pointwise on $\partial\Omega$; and $V=\{u\in X:\operatorname{div}u=0\}$, $H=\overline V^{\,L^2}$. This is the explicit weak perfect-electric-conductor class of that item, not an identification with every maximal tangential-trace realisation.

Then:

(a) **Smooth PEC cavity.** The curl form $(u,v)\mapsto\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u\cdot\operatorname{curl}v$ on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis $\{u_j\}$ with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity, with $\lambda_j\to\infty$ whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional and with the finite-dimensional zero eigenspace retained. Each eigenfield $u_j\in V$ satisfies $\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u_j\cdot\operatorname{curl}v=\lambda_j\int_\Omega u_j\cdot v$ for every $v\in X$; the eigen-equation $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ holds distributionally together with the PEC trace; and $u_j$ has a $C^\infty$ representative on $\overline\Omega$ for which $\operatorname{div}u_j=0$, $\nu\times u_j=0$ and $\partial_\nu u_{j,n}+(\operatorname{div}\nu)u_{j,n}=0$ hold classically on $\partial\Omega$, where $u_{j,n}=u_j\cdot\nu$ and $\nu$ is extended constant along collar normal lines. For every explicitly chosen positive mathematical speed $v_{\mathrm{wave}}>0$ and every pair of data $q_0\in V$, $q_1\in H$, the associated second-order wave has coefficients solving $a_j''+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_ja_j=0$ with $a_j(0)=\langle q_0,u_j\rangle$ and $a_j'(0)=\langle q_1,u_j\rangle$, in the modal class of that item: its displacement lies in $C(\mathbb R;V)$ and its velocity in $C(\mathbb R;H)$, finite modal sums converge in $C(K;V)$ and $C(K;H)$ on every compact time interval $K$, and the finitely many $\lambda_j=0$ modes are $a_j(t)=a_j(0)+ta_j'(0)$. The speed is a positive abstract mathematical parameter and has no physical dependency. The scalar auxiliary Dirichlet resolvent used inside the recorded cavity argument has, for every $q\in L^2(\Omega)$, a unique solution $\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap H^2(\Omega)$ of $(1-\Delta)\varphi=q$, with smooth zero-boundary approximants converging in $H^2$ and whose gradients converge in the PEC graph norm, by [[lem-em-dirichlet-resolvent-h-two-and-smooth-test-density]]. For smooth $q$ this solution is smooth on the closure by the same smooth-boundary bootstrap; no classical regularity for a general $L^2$ datum is asserted. Smooth unshifted scalar boundary problems have the classical upgrade of [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]] with $\varepsilon=I$.

(b) **Rectangular reflection-parity class.** Let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L_j>0$ and let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ be constants. In the reflection boundary class of [[lem-em-rectangular-pec-energy-completeness]] (real $L^2$ fields on the torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$ whose components carry the parities of that item and whose distributional divergences vanish), the finite separated Fourier modes are dense at every time, and every initial datum of the class has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the class, along which $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ is constant.

No completeness is asserted in lossy, open-ended or non-smooth classes, and the constant-Ohmic and open-longitudinal branches are homed separately as physical items on the guide page; they are not mathematical premises or dependencies of this statement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The sphere trace and its harmonic extension. On $S^2$ the outward unit normal is $\nu(n)=n$, so the normal derivative of $x_3$ is $\partial_nx_3=\nabla x_3\cdot n=e_3\cdot n=n_3$; thus $x_3$ is harmonic on $\mathbb R^3$ by [F1] and has boundary trace $f(n)=n_3$ on $S^2$. The function $f$ is continuous, hence in $L^2(S^2)$ with coefficients $f_{lm}$, so the ball boundary branch [F7] applies: the series $\sum_{l,m}r^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ is the unique harmonic function on $B_1$ with $L^2$ boundary limit $f$ and continuous extension to $\overline B_1$. Since $x_3$ is such a harmonic function, the branch identifies the extension as $u(x)=x_3$; in particular $f=n_3$ is an admissible ball-boundary datum, not an excluded class.

The total mass of the sphere measure. Apply the polar-coordinates identity [F3] with $n=3$ to the indicator of the closed unit ball, a Borel measurable function: $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\mathbf 1_{\overline B_1}\,d\lambda_3=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^2}\mathbf 1_{\overline B_1}(r\omega)r^2\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr$; the left side is $\lambda_3(\overline B_1)=4\pi/3$ by [F4], and on the right side $\mathbf 1_{\overline B_1}(r\omega)=1$ for $0\le r\le1$ and every $\omega\in S^2$, so the iterated integral is $\bigl(\int_0^1r^2\,dr\bigr)\sigma(S^2)=\sigma(S^2)/3$; hence $\sigma(S^2)=3\cdot4\pi/3=4\pi$. The argument uses the Countable Choice assumption of the polar identity [F3].

The piecewise-linear function and its weak derivatives. Define $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ by $u(x)=x_1$ for $x_1<0$ and $u(x)=x_1/2$ for $x_1>0$. Assign $u=0$ on the interface $\{x_1=0\}$; both branches tend to $0$ as $x_1\to0$ through their sides, so $u$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^3$, and it is $C^\infty$ on each of the two open half-spaces. Its distributional first derivatives are the locally integrable — indeed bounded — functions $g_1:=\mathbf 1_{\{x_1<0\}}+\tfrac12\mathbf 1_{\{x_1>0\}}$, $g_2=0$, $g_3=0$: for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, integrating by parts on each half-space with the vanishing of the boundary terms (the traces $x_1\varphi$ and $\tfrac12x_1\varphi$ vanish on $\{x_1=0\}$ and at infinity) gives $\int u\,\partial_1\varphi=-\int g_1\varphi$, and the partial derivatives in the other two coordinates vanish identically on each side. Hence the weak first derivatives of $u$ are represented by $g_1,g_2,g_3$, so $u$ satisfies the weak-differentiability part of the definitions in [F6]; and $u$ is not $C^1$ on any neighbourhood of the interface, since its classical one-sided derivatives $1$ and $1/2$ in the $x_1$ direction differ at every point of $\{x_1=0\}$.

The weak transmission equation. With $\varepsilon=1$ on $\{x_1<0\}$ and $\varepsilon=2$ on $\{x_1>0\}$, the field $\varepsilon
abla u$ takes the value $(1,0,0)$ on both sides: on the first side $\varepsilon\partial_1u=1\cdot1=1$ and on the second $\varepsilon\partial_1u=2\cdot	frac12=1$, with the other components zero. Hence $\varepsilon
abla u$ is the constant field $\mathbf c=(1,0,0)$, whose divergence is $0$ by [F2]; equivalently, for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ one has $\int(\varepsilon
abla u)\cdot
abla\varphi\,dx=\int\mathbf c\cdot
abla\varphi\,dx=0$, so the distributional equation $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon
abla u)=0$ holds weakly on $\mathbb R^3$. Thus the weak formulation of the transmission problem is satisfied by a function that is not $C^1$, and its one-sided first derivatives jump from $1$ to $1/2$ across the interface.

Incompatibility of the two sphere conditions. Suppose $w\in C^2(\overline B_1)$ satisfied $\Delta w=0$ in $B_1$ and $\partial_nw=1$ on $S^2$, and apply the divergence theorem [F5] to $F=\nabla w\in C^1(\overline B_1;\mathbb R^3)$ on the bounded $C^1$ domain $B_1$: $0=\int_{B_1}\Delta w\,dx=\int_{S^2}\partial_nw\,d\sigma=\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ by [F1] and step 1.2, a contradiction. Hence no such $w$ exists, so the conditions are incompatible; by step 1.1 the same trace $f=n_3$ is nevertheless an admissible ball-boundary datum whose harmonic extension has normal derivative $n_3$, not the constant $1$.

Scope of the elliptic conclusions. Step 2.1 produces a weak solution of $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon\nabla u)=0$ for a coefficient that is positive and smooth on each open side but discontinuous across the interface $\{x_1=0\}$, and step 1.3 shows the solution fails to be $C^1$ near the interface; this is a local smooth-interface witness with smooth coefficients on each closed side, and its one-sided regularity is explicit from the affine formulas. It illustrates the distinction made in [F8], but the global transmission theorem is not directly invoked: the plane is unbounded and is not a closed interface strictly inside a bounded domain as that theorem requires. Therefore a global $C^1$ or $C^\infty$-on-the-closure conclusion for the piecewise-constant coefficient case is false, while the recorded one-sided piecewise regularity is the sharp conclusion; the smooth-coefficient statements of that theorem cannot be extended to this case.

Scope of the spectral completeness conclusions. The coefficient field of steps 1.3 and 2.1 is discontinuous across $\{x_1=0\}$ and its weak solution is not classical $C^1$ there, so the configuration is not one of the smooth classical configurations to which the smooth PEC cavity or rectangular classes of [F9] refer; that theorem declares its smooth-domain class and asserts in its statement that no completeness is asserted in non-smooth classes. The explicit weak solution of step 2.1 shows that the weak formulation of the equation remains valid in this excluded configuration and does not acquire the missing classical regularity, so it cannot be used to extend the spectral conclusions. This scalar transmission witness is not itself a vector PEC eigenfield and makes no claim that spectral completeness fails in any other correctly specified weak class; [F9] is used to inspect the stated scope, not to infer such a failure.

Audit. Step 1.1 identifies the admissible ball-boundary datum $f=n_3$ and its harmonic extension; step 1.2 computes the sphere mass $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ from the polar formula and the closed-ball volume; step 2.2 uses the divergence theorem to show that $\Delta u=0$ in $B_1$ and $\partial_nu=1$ on $S^2$ cannot hold simultaneously; steps 1.3 and 2.1 exhibit the continuous, weakly differentiable piecewise-linear solution with $\varepsilon\partial_1u\equiv1$ and show that it is not $C^1$; and steps 3.1 and 3.2 place this witness against the exact hypotheses of the elliptic and spectral results. The elliptic and spectral citations [F8]-[F9] are used solely to compare their stated hypotheses and exclusions; their Axiom-of-Choice existence conclusions are not invoked here. Countable Choice is used through the ball-boundary supplier [F7], the polar-coordinate identity [F3] of step 1.2 and the divergence theorem [F5] of step 2.2, whose own assumptions are those of the Statement; no other choice principle is used. No measurement, physical field interpretation or empirical claim is made.

boundaries.reason: No empty object occurs: the unit ball has nonempty interior and boundary, the interface x_1=0 is nonempty, and every integral in steps 1.1-2.2 is over a nonempty set.

boundaries.evidence: The zero cases are computed rather than assumed: f=0 and u=0 satisfy their formulas, while the contradiction of step 2.2 uses the strictly positive mass sigma(S^2)=4 pi obtained in step 1.2.

Single-object cases drive the example: step 1.3 computes the one weak derivative vector (1,1/2,0) of the piecewise-linear function, and step 2.1 shows epsilon grad u is the one constant field (1,0,0).

The degeneracy is the example's subject: the coefficient jumps from 1 to 2 and the derivative from 1 to 1/2 across the interface x_1=0, which steps 3.1 and 3.2 place against the exact smooth hypotheses.

boundaries.reason: No interval endpoint, boundary endpoint or limit at infinity is charged: the computations are pointwise on R^3 and on the closed unit ball and sphere, with the boundary terms evaluated by the divergence theorem in step 2.2.

boundaries.evidence: Countable Choice is assumed in the example and used through the polar-coordinate identity [F3] in step 1.2 and the divergence theorem [F5] in step 2.2, as recorded in the audit step 4.1.

boundaries.reason: The example proves incompatibility of two conditions and identifies a hypothesis boundary; it asserts no biconditional, so there is no forward equivalence direction.
No converse is asserted: the example does not claim that every non-smooth coefficient configuration fails the conclusions, only that this explicit configuration lies outside the smooth classes.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L>0$ and $R=(0,L_1)\times(0,L_2)$ with $L_1,L_2>0$.
(a) [One interval] The families $\{\cos(m\pi x/L)\}_{m\ge0}$ and $\{\sin(m\pi x/L)\}_{m\ge1}$ are orthogonal complete systems in the real Hilbert space $L^2(0,L)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]): each is orthogonal, and its closed linear span is all of $L^2(0,L)$.
(b) [Rectangle] With $m,n$ ranging over $\mathbb N_0$ in cosine slots and over $\mathbb N_{\ge1}$ in sine slots, each of the four product families $\{\cos\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\cos\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$, $\{\cos\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\sin\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$, $\{\sin\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\cos\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$ and $\{\sin\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\sin\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$ is an orthogonal complete system in $L^2(R)$; in particular the Neumann family $\{h_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge0}$ and the Dirichlet family $\{e_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge1}$ of [[lem-em-rectangle-mode-profile-identities]] are orthogonal complete systems in $L^2(R)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L_j>0$ and let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ be constants. Define the reflection boundary class by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2,x_3$-walls, and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$; extend $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$, cyclically for $B_2,B_3$. Work on the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$ in the real $L^2$ fields with these parities and distributional $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$. For smooth fields the parity class gives $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on $\partial Q$. Then: (i) the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in this class, and the class is complete for the $L^2$ pairing ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]); (ii) for every initial datum in the class there is a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the same class ([[def-distributional-derivative]]); (iii) the energy $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ is constant along the solution. This is an explicit weak PEC model; it supplies neither trace regularity for arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ fields nor completeness in lossy, open or non-rectangular guides.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its SI units and its fields $E,B$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-fields]]. Fix $a,b>0$, write $x_t=(x_1,x_2)$, $e_z:=e_3$, and define $\nabla_t f=(\partial_1f,\partial_2f,0)$, $\Delta_t f=\partial_1^2f+\partial_2^2f$ and $\operatorname{div}_tu_t=\partial_1u_1+\partial_2u_2$ for the stated regularity, using [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].
(a) [Straight guide] A straight guide region is $\Omega_A:=A\times\mathbb R$ where $A$ is either a bounded connected $C^1$ plane domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]) or the explicit rectangular cross-section; the rectangle has corners and is treated by its open faces, not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, with longitudinal axis $e_z$; for a rectangular cross-section $A=R_{ab}:=(0,a)\times(0,b)$ the region is called the rectangular guide and its walls are the four open faces $\{x_1=0\},\{x_1=a\},\{x_2=0\},\{x_2=b\}$. A rectangular cavity region is $\Omega_c:=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ for fixed $d>0$, with the six open faces as its walls. The separate smooth-cavity spectral branch uses an explicitly declared bounded $C^\infty$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ with its smooth PEC boundary; it is not the rectangular reflection class. Spatial derivatives are taken at fixed $t$; the fields are defined on $\Omega\times I$ with the regularity declared by each theorem.
(b) [PEC boundary model] On every open wall (a wall minus its edges) the ideal perfectly conducting boundary model declares the two conditions $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$, where $n$ is the outward unit normal of that wall ($-e_1,+e_1,-e_2,+e_2$ on the four rectangular walls, and $\pm e_j$ on the six cavity walls). Its physical reading is the ideal-conductor limit of the stationary interface conditions of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]: with $E=B=0$ inside the ideal conductor the tangential electric field and the normal magnetic field vanish, while the surface-charge and surface-current readings $\sigma_f=-n\cdot D$ and $K_f=-n\times H$ for the filling-side traces (the wall normal points from the filling into the conductor, so the jump is $0$ minus the filling trace) are determined by the traces and are not prescribed here. The supplier's hypotheses (a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with one-sided $C^1$ fields) cover a smooth stationary interface, not the $\sigma\to\infty$ idealization nor the box edges; the guide/cavity conditions on the open walls are therefore declared as an idealization of this definition, and no pointwise statement on the edges is made.
(c) [Zero-normal-B reflection class] For the rectangular box $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L=(a,b,d)$, the reflection class is the class of locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $Q$ whose extensions to the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$, defined by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2$-, $x_3$-walls and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$, and extending $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$ and cyclically for $B_2,B_3$, are $L^2$ fields, together with the distributional constraints that $\operatorname{div}E$ and $\operatorname{div}B$ vanish on the torus for the extensions. This is the declared weak PEC model used for the cavity initial-value problem; for smooth fields the parities give $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on $\partial Q$. Initial data not in this class (for example data with trapped normal $B$) are excluded, as are the general $H(\operatorname{curl})$ boundary classes, which are defined by the mathematical suppliers and are not identified here with the classical conditions.
(d) [TE, TM, TEM] For a guide or cavity field $(E,B)$, the longitudinal components are $E_z:=E\cdot e_z$ and $B_z:=B\cdot e_z$; the field is called TE (transverse electric) if $E_z\equiv0$, TM (transverse magnetic) if $B_z\equiv0$, and TEM if both vanish, always relative to the named axis $e_z$.
(e) [Separated phasor convention] For $\omega>0$ and $\beta\in\mathbb C$, a $\beta$-$\omega$ separated phasor field on the guide is a real field of the form $F(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\tilde F(x_1,x_2)e^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with a complex amplitude $\tilde F$, componentwise; $\omega/(2\pi)$ is the frequency and $\beta$ the longitudinal propagation constant; when $\beta$ is real, $\beta>0$ describes propagation in the $+e_z$ direction under this phase convention, while a complex $\beta$ gives the spatial factor $e^{-\operatorname{Im}\beta x_3}$ and may grow in the opposite direction; each consuming branch states its selection.
(f) [Scope] The definition fixes the geometry, the PEC boundary model, the weak reflection class and the mode terminology; it asserts no field equation, no constitutive law and no existence or completeness of modes, Rectangular TE/TM candidates and the rectangular reflection class, declared smooth bounded PEC cavity spectral classes, and smooth straight-guide TEM potential branches (including the coaxial annulus) are within this geometry. No general non-rectangular TE/TM guide theory, circular-guide spectral classification, open-end or junction scattering, or arbitrary lossy model is supplied. The same stationary PEC geometry also hosts the explicitly declared constant scalar Ohmic cavity class and the full longitudinal finite-energy reflection class of the straight rectangular guide; constitutive and evolution claims belong to their consuming theorems, not this definition.

**Conventions fixed by this definition.** The definition records objects and conditions only: the guide and cavity regions, their open walls and outward normals, the ideal PEC boundary conditions with their interface reading and excluded idealization, the zero-normal-$B$ reflection class with its distributional divergence constraints, the axis-relative TE/TM/TEM terminology, and the separated phasor encoding of real fields. It asserts no field equation, no constitutive relation, no existence, uniqueness or completeness of modes, and no dissipation or energy claim; those belong to the consuming theorems, each of which restates the branch of the material model it uses. The rectangular cross-section is treated through its four open faces and is not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, and no pointwise condition on box edges is made.

Restate the class conventions of [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]]: $L^2:=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is the real Hilbert space of square integrable vector fields with the inner product $\langle u,v\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot v\,dx$ induced by the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and
$$H(\operatorname{curl})=\{u\in L^2:\operatorname{curl}u\in L^2\},\qquad H(\operatorname{div})=\{u\in L^2:\operatorname{div}u\in L^2\}$$
are the graph spaces with norms $\|u\|^2_{H(\operatorname{curl})}=\|u\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_2^2$ and $\|u\|^2_{H(\operatorname{div})}=\|u\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}u\|_2^2$, the curl and divergence being taken in the distributional sense; $X$ is the graph-norm closure in $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$ of the fields that are smooth on a neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$ and satisfy $\nu\times u=0$ pointwise on $\partial\Omega$; and $V=\{u\in X:\operatorname{div}u=0\}$, $H=\overline V^{\,L^2}$. Then:

(a) **Smooth PEC cavity.** The curl form $(u,v)\mapsto\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u\cdot\operatorname{curl}v$ on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis $\{u_j\}$ with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity, with $\lambda_j\to\infty$ whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional and with the finite-dimensional zero eigenspace retained. Each eigenfield $u_j\in V$ satisfies $\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u_j\cdot\operatorname{curl}v=\lambda_j\int_\Omega u_j\cdot v$ for every $v\in X$; the eigen-equation $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ holds distributionally together with the PEC trace; and $u_j$ has a $C^\infty$ representative on $\overline\Omega$ for which $\operatorname{div}u_j=0$, $\nu\times u_j=0$ and $\partial_\nu u_{j,n}+(\operatorname{div}\nu)u_{j,n}=0$ hold classically on $\partial\Omega$, where $u_{j,n}=u_j\cdot\nu$ and $\nu$ is extended constant along collar normal lines. For every explicitly chosen positive mathematical speed $v_{\mathrm{wave}}>0$ and every pair of data $q_0\in V$, $q_1\in H$, the associated second-order wave has coefficients solving $a_j''+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_ja_j=0$ with $a_j(0)=\langle q_0,u_j\rangle$ and $a_j'(0)=\langle q_1,u_j\rangle$, in the modal class of that item: its displacement lies in $C(\mathbb R;V)$ and its velocity in $C(\mathbb R;H)$, finite modal sums converge in $C(K;V)$ and $C(K;H)$ on every compact time interval $K$, and the finitely many $\lambda_j=0$ modes are $a_j(t)=a_j(0)+ta_j'(0)$. The speed is a positive abstract mathematical parameter and has no physical dependency. The scalar auxiliary Dirichlet resolvent used inside the recorded cavity argument has, for every $q\in L^2(\Omega)$, a unique solution $\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap H^2(\Omega)$ of $(1-\Delta)\varphi=q$, with smooth zero-boundary approximants converging in $H^2$ and whose gradients converge in the PEC graph norm, by [[lem-em-dirichlet-resolvent-h-two-and-smooth-test-density]]. For smooth $q$ this solution is smooth on the closure by the same smooth-boundary bootstrap; no classical regularity for a general $L^2$ datum is asserted. Smooth unshifted scalar boundary problems have the classical upgrade of [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]] with $\varepsilon=I$.

(b) **Rectangular reflection-parity class.** Let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L_j>0$ and let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ be constants. In the reflection boundary class of [[lem-em-rectangular-pec-energy-completeness]] (real $L^2$ fields on the torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$ whose components carry the parities of that item and whose distributional divergences vanish), the finite separated Fourier modes are dense at every time, and every initial datum of the class has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the class, along which $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ is constant.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be an embedded smooth submanifold. Then there is a
positive smooth function $\delta:S\to(0,\infty)$ such that the restricted
normal addition map
$$E:\Omega_\delta\to\mathbb R^m,\qquad \Omega_\delta:=\{(p,v)\in N^\perp S:\|v\|<\delta(p)\},$$
is a diffeomorphism onto an open neighbourhood of $S$. In particular, $S$ has a
tubular neighbourhood in $\mathbb R^m$.

Let $\beta$ be the standard flat function. The **standard smooth step function** is
$$ \sigma(t):=\frac{\beta(t)}{\beta(t)+\beta(1-t)}. $$
Because $\beta$ is smooth and positive on $(0,\infty)$, the denominator is positive on $(0,1)$, while $\sigma(t)=0$ for $t\le 0$ and $\sigma(t)=1$ for $t\ge 1$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]]: constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (isotropic scalar case included) with $D=\varepsilon E$ and $B=\mu H$, and the conduction relation $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ with $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite and a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Assume the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the regularity hypotheses of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], so that its macroscopic equations hold on $\Omega\times I$. Define the stored-energy density and the energy-flux vector

$$u:=\tfrac12\bigl(E\cdot D+B\cdot H\bigr),\qquad S:=E\times H,$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; $u$ carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $S$ carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Then:

**(a) [Local balance and positivity]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J_f\cdot E.$$

Moreover $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot\varepsilon E+H\cdot\mu H)\ge0$, with $u(x,t)>0$ whenever $(E(x,t),H(x,t))\ne(0,0)$.

**(b) [Dissipation reading]** With $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite, $E\cdot\sigma E\ge0$ and the balance reads

$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S+E\cdot\sigma E=-J_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot E;$$

the nonnegative term $E\cdot\sigma E$ is the Ohmic dissipation density of the model.

**(c) [Fixed-volume balance]** Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with $\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let $t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) as in that divergence theorem, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal of $\partial\Omega'$. Then for every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u(x,t)\,dx=-\int_{\Omega'}J_f\cdot E\,dx-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S\cdot n\,dS.$$

**(d) [Scope]** The density $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$ is a stored-energy density only for this constant symmetric nondispersive model; for general dispersive, nonlocal, nonlinear or hysteretic response no instantaneous stored-energy density is defined or claimed by this item, and the general dispersive work balance is not supplied. The identities hold only where the fields and sources have the stated regularity, the fixed-volume form keeps its boundary term, and no conservation of $\int_{\Omega'}u$ is asserted unless that term vanishes. No empirical claim is made.

derivations.claim:
[Clause (a)] The families $\{h_{mn}\}$ and $\{e_{mn}\}$ are orthogonal complete systems in $L^2(R_{ab})$ by [F1], which gives the expansion statement. Each member with $(m,n)
e(0,0)$ has zero integral over $R_{ab}$ by the orthogonality of [F1] against $h_{00}=1$, so the closed linear span $S$ of $\{h_{mn}:(m,n)
e(0,0)\}$ is contained in the closed zero-mean subspace $Z=\{f\in L^2(R_{ab}):\int_{R_{ab}}f=0\}$; conversely, if $f\in Z$, the expansion theorem [F1] applied to the complete orthonormal family obtained by normalizing all the $h_{mn}$ writes $f$ as the norm limit of its finite partial sums, and the coefficient of $h_{00}$ is $\langle f,h_{00}angle/\|h_{00}\|^2=\int_{R_{ab}}f/ab=0$, so those partial sums use only indices $(m,n)
e(0,0)$ and $f\in S$. Hence $S=Z$: the remaining Neumann profiles are complete in the zero-mean subspace and not in all of $L^2(R_{ab})$ because the constant function is orthogonal to them and nonzero. The constant $h_{00}=1$ stays in the full mathematical basis, while the physical TE candidate family excludes it by the Maxwell index restriction of [[pthm-em-rectangular-mode-candidates]] (c), so no nonzero positive-frequency TE reconstruction is asserted from the constant scalar profile; the Dirichlet profiles keep their full scalar completeness.

[Clause (b)] By [F2] the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in the rectangular reflection class at every time, every initial datum in the class has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of the lossless first-order system in the class, and the energy $\frac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)$ is constant along the solution; this distributional system is the explicitly adopted weak material evolution of the reflection model. The energy equals $\int_Qu$ for the weak stored-energy density $u=\frac12(\varepsilon|E|^2+\mu^{-1}|B|^2)$ of [F5], which is defined almost everywhere and nonnegative; its integrability and constancy are furnished by the supplier, and no nonlinear weak Poynting identity is asserted. Finally, the four macroscopic equations with $D=\varepsilon E$ and $H=B/\mu$ follow distributionally from the two evolution equations and the divergence constraints of the class: $\operatorname{div}D=\varepsilon\operatorname{div}E=0$ and $\operatorname{div}B=0$ are the class constraints, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ is the second evolution equation, and $\operatorname{curl}H=\mu^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B=\mu^{-1}(\varepsilon\mu)\partial_tE=\partial_tD$ uses the first evolution equation $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$.

[Clause (c), spectral content] Assume the full Axiom of Choice as in [F3], let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ cavity and let $X,V,H$, $\{u_j\}$, $\lambda_j\ge0$ be the classes and eigenbasis of [F3]. Then the curl form on $V$ has the complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis with nonnegative finite-multiplicity eigenvalues tending to infinity when $H$ is infinite dimensional and a finite-dimensional zero eigenspace retained; the eigen-equation holds distributionally with the PEC trace, each $u_j$ has a $C^\infty$ representative on the closure, and the full-$X$ variational identity holds for every $v\in X$. With $v_{\mathrm{wave}}=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}>0$, the associated second-order electric wave has displacement in $C(\mathbb R;V)$ and velocity in $C(\mathbb R;H)$ for arbitrary initial data in $V\times H$, finite modal sums converge in these norms uniformly on compact times, and its zero eigenmodes may be affine in time. These are the spectral and wave assertions of [F3], taken with the exact hypotheses of the suppliers.

[Clause (c), first-order modal equation] Let $J$ be an open time interval and let a strong first-order solution obey the hypotheses of the Statement: $E\in C^1(J;H)\cap C(J;V)$, $B\in C^1(J;L^2)\cap C(J;H(\operatorname{curl}))$, with the first-order equations holding as $L^2$ identities and both distributional divergence constraints, the magnetic normal-zero condition $\int_\Omega B(t)\cdot\nabla\psi=0$ for every smooth scalar $\psi$ on the closure, and $E(t)\in V$ encoding the electric tangential-zero data; no magnetic membership in $X$ is assumed. Put $a_j(t):=\langle E(t),u_j\rangle$. To pair $\operatorname{curl}B$ against the smooth eigenfield $u_j$, use the collar cutoff of [F4]: write $s$ for the inward normal coordinate in a tubular neighbourhood of the compact boundary, so that $|n\times u_j|\le Cs$ in the collar because $u_j$ is smooth on the closure with $n\times u_j=0$, and let $\eta_\delta$ be the standard smooth step with $\eta_\delta=0$ for $s\le\delta$ and $1$ for $s\ge2\delta$. Then $\eta_\delta u_j\to u_j$ and $\operatorname{curl}(\eta_\delta u_j)\to\operatorname{curl}u_j$ in $L^2$ as $\delta\to0$, since the derivative-cutoff term is supported on a layer of volume $O(\delta)$ and is bounded by $C/\delta$ times $O(s)$; the distributional identity of [F4] on the compactly supported smooth test $\eta_\delta u_j$ gives $\langle\operatorname{curl}B,\eta_\delta u_j\rangle=\langle B,\operatorname{curl}(\eta_\delta u_j)\rangle$, and Cauchy–Schwarz with the two limits gives $\langle\operatorname{curl}B,u_j\rangle=\langle B,\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle$ for the actual graph-regular field $B$. Hence $a_j'=\langle E',u_j\rangle=v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\langle\operatorname{curl}B,u_j\rangle=v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\langle B,\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle$ on $J$. The assumed $B\in C^1(J;L^2)$ permits one further derivative: $a_j''=v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\langle B',\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle=-v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\langle\operatorname{curl}E,\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle=-v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_j\langle E,u_j\rangle$, where the last equality is the full-$X$ eigenvariational identity of [F3] tested at $v=E(t)\in V\subset X$; thus $a_j''+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_ja_j=0$, and $a_j$ is $C^2$ because $E$ and $B$ are $C^1$ in their norms. If $\lambda_j=0$, the same identity at $v=u_j$ gives $\|\operatorname{curl}u_j\|_2^2=0$, so $\operatorname{curl}u_j=0$ and $a_j'=v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\langle B,\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle=0$: the electric zero modes are constant under first-order Maxwell evolution, while the unrestricted second-order wave of step 1.3 retains its affine zero modes. This distinguishes first-order Maxwell data from arbitrary second-order $V\times H$ data; the pairing imposed no magnetic electric-type trace, and the divergence constraints and the declared weak magnetic normal condition remain part of the model.

[Clause (d)] Clause (a) is step 1.1, clause (b) is step 1.2, and clause (c) is steps 1.3 and 2.1. Completeness is asserted only for the transverse $L^2$ profiles and for the two declared cavity classes with their exact hypotheses; this lossless theorem does not itself supply the longitudinal expansion or the dissipative evolution, which are supplied separately by [[pthm-em-open-rectangular-guide-completeness]] and [[pthm-em-uniform-ohmic-modal-decay]]. None of the statements supplies arbitrary lossy, dispersive, open-end scattering, non-smooth or exterior problems, or arbitrary non-rectangular guide problems beyond the declared smooth-cavity spectral class; no trace regularity for arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ fields and no identification of the weak classes with every maximal tangential-trace realization is asserted, and the zero eigenvalues and zero modes are retained throughout. The inherited Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice cover the spectral, Fourier and collar suppliers, and no lossy or open-domain step was made.
